A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HUME and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. The original experiments and supporting material can be matched reliably despite substantial additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original human annotations, inter-annotator agreement, and comparisons with 13 embedding models across 16 datasets and 26 task-language pairs.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds evaluations of nine LLM annotators, human–LLM difficulty correlations, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: HUME's annotation interfaces, sampling framework, and alignment with embedding-evaluation metrics are retained. The prompted LLMs constitute an additional comparison arm, while the expanded description of human instructions does not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 16 datasets, four task categories, five languages, and 26 task-language pairs. The new LLM study evaluates 19 existing classification, reranking, and STS pairs; clustering remains in the human–embedding comparison.

E2.justification: v3 retains all 13 embedding comparators and adds nine evaluated LLM annotators: GPT-5 and GPT-4.1 full/mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Mistral Small-24B-Instruct, and three Qwen3 variants. Their results appear in Table 2 and Appendix I, substantially extending the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 3.6 introduces a substantial automated-annotation evaluation arm: LLMs receive the human task instances and instructions and produce labels, similarity scores, or document rankings. This comparison excludes clustering and aggregates 19 task-language pairs. The original human sample sizes, annotator allocation, and primary metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix I.1 adds a supplementary analysis of whether humans and LLMs encounter similar task difficulties, using correlations across 19 task-language pairs. Existing dataset-error case studies, agreement analyses, and human–model gap analyses are retained, sometimes relocated; no new ablation or distribution-shift study is introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports agreement metrics and annotator counts but no performance confidence intervals. v3 Appendix E reports 95% intervals for all 26 task-language pairs using Wilson intervals, Fisher transformations, and annotator ranges, with significance flags based on interval exclusion. Appendix I also adds correlation p-values. These additions do not establish increased annotation or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: The original aggregate and per-dataset human–embedding tables retain their numerical results. v3 adds extensive LLM scores, including GPT-4.1-mini at 76.1 versus humans at 81.2 on the 19-pair subset, an overall difficulty correlation of 0.52, and reported significant human–model differences on 14 of 26 pairs. The 81.2 human score is a different aggregation from the retained 77.6 overall score.

T1.justification: No new formal definitions, theoretical assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced. The added confidence-interval procedures are empirical statistical methodology, and the retrieval-proxy explanation is conceptual motivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a substantive contribution concerning whether LLMs can replace human annotators, concluding that they should augment human evaluation. The original HUME contribution and headline human–embedding comparison of 77.6 versus 80.1 remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of LLM annotation weaknesses and limitations concerning demographic coverage, unavailable original annotation protocols, and unexplained performance gaps. Section 5.1 changes v1's acknowledgment that mechanisms remain unclear into a claim that the evidence confirms annotation-artifact fitting. Section 5.3 also newly qualifies that disagreement can reflect natural judgment variability rather than dataset defects.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 newly documents deriving instructions from dataset papers and piloting them, while Section 6.1 identifies annotators as consenting co-authors. These improve procedural disclosure without establishing that the original annotations were redone. Existing code, dataset, leaderboard access information, and embedding-model specifications are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work sections are essentially unchanged. v3 adds Basile et al. (2021) on disagreement and Fisher (1915) and Wilson (1927) for statistical methodology, providing limited additional context rather than substantially revising the relationship to prior embedding research.

P1.justification: v3 substantially restructures the narrative with separate instruction and LLM-evaluation sections, rewritten discussion and limitations, condensed task summaries, and revised opening and closing sections. The appendices are reorganized to accommodate dataset specifications, statistical analysis, and LLM results, while much existing supporting text is preserved.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with reordered tasks, a percentage axis, and new visual encodings. The dataset table moves to Appendix A, and the main-text win-rate figure moves to Appendix G. Six tables are added for LLM summaries, detailed scores, confidence intervals, and correlations; the existing annotation screenshots and other analytical plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful LLM comparisons, supported difficulty correlations, and clearer procedural and limitation disclosures. However, Appendix E does not justify treating annotator ranges as 95% confidence intervals and reports nonzero intervals for single-annotator tasks under that stated methodology. Section 5.1 also replaces an explicit mechanistic uncertainty with a stronger artifact-fitting claim without a corresponding causal test. These weaknesses affect the new statistical and interpretive conclusions, so the benefits and harms do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.
